healthcare-workers-what-they-learn-to-ca.author: Christopher Perkins, BSN, RN
healthcare-workers-what-they-learn-to-ca.core: Posted in last 7 days Healthcare Workers - What They Learn to Call Normal Some things become routine in healthcare long before they should ever become acceptable. We miss meals. We move from witnessing a family’s worst moment to caring for the next patient. We work through exhaustion, staffing challenges, grief, and circumstances that most people will never experience. And somewhere along the way, we begin calling these things normal. I’m grateful to have my latest article, “What Healthcare Workers Learn to Call Normal,” published in the Journal of Nursing (RN-Journal). This piece is about more than burnout. It’s about the complicated relationship many of us have with the work we do. Healthcare has given me experiences, relationships, and a sense of purpose that I wouldn’t trade. But it has also shown me how easily we can mistake our ability to endure difficult conditions for evidence that those conditions are acceptable. As a nurse and healthcare leader, I believe we need to have more conversations about that distinction. Just because healthcare workers have learned to carry something doesn’t mean they should have to. I’m also continuing to explore these experiences through Good in a Crisis, a nonfiction book project examining what healthcare gives us, what it takes from us, and what needs to change. And I want to hear from you. Whether you’re a nurse, physician, respiratory therapist, technician, paramedic, or another healthcare professional, your experiences matter. The difficult moments, the meaningful ones, the things you’ve carried home, and the things you’ve never said out loud. I’m inviting healthcare workers to participate in a voluntary questionnaire, with the option to remain anonymous. Read my published article: https://lnkd.in/gx8TetgU Share your experience for Good in a Crisis: https://lnkd.in/gpzUmKTn Because the people who spend their lives caring for others deserve to have their stories heard, too. #Nursing #HealthcareLeadership #HealthcareWorkers #NurseWellbeing #GoodInACrisis

If you appealed a removal, suspension, demotion or layoff to the Ohio State Personnel Board of Review, or appealed a denied unemployment claim to the Unemployment Compensation Review Commission, I would like to hear from you. How far it went - intake, hearing, decision, appeal. How the job ended: you resigned, you were fired, or you left because the conditions had become something you could no longer work under. Those two bodies sit at the end of the line. By the time someone reaches them the concern has usually already been through the employer, the internal channel and at least one state office, so the file holds the whole route in compressed form. State of Ohio is where the work is. If you went through the equivalent body in another state or another country, write to me anyway. The data comparison is the point. If you are under a settlement, please read it before you write. The right to speak to a government agency or to your own attorney survives most of that language. A private message is enough, and you do not need to identify your case publicly. Did your employer make false statements to a state body? What was the worst tactic they used in their defense? Did you obtain the hearing transcript? I also welcome connections with #whistleblower advocates, #investigative journalists, #watchdog organizations, #researchers, and #attorneys interested in this work. classical-musicians-and-fans-practice-ro.core: Posted in last 7 days Classical Musicians & Fans - Practice Room Confessions Welcome to Practice Room Tea! ☕️ Have Some Classical Music Tea? Spill It Here! Have some classical music tea? Because I want to hear ALL about it! Hi everyone! I'm Ayla Rose, an opera singer and the creator of Practice Room Tea, a new podcast spilling the tea, one note at a time. I've always loved classical music, but I've noticed that a lot of people think it's boring or just something you listen to when you're trying to fall asleep. And honestly, I get it! But what people don't realize is just how much drama and scandal there is in the classical music world. Some of these composers could seriously give Netflix a run for its money. That's actually one of the reasons I wanted to start this podcast. I want to make classical music a little less intimidating and a lot more entertaining. Whether you've been studying music your entire life or couldn't tell Mozart from Mahler, I want there to be something for everyone. The first episodes of Practice Room Tea will start coming out in December! I'm still getting everything ready, and in the meantime, I would LOVE to hear from you guys. I'm looking for funny stories, questions, personal experiences, and ideas for future episodes. I also really want this podcast to be something people can participate in, instead of just listening to me talk for an hour about composers who have been dead for 200 years. Here's some of the tea I'm looking for: Practice Room Confessions: Rehearsal disasters, embarrassing auditions, performances where everything went wrong, or just something completely ridiculous that's happened to you as a musician. I feel like we all have at least one story that still haunts us. Classical Music Scandals: Composer drama, historical gossip, ridiculous rivalries, and stories that deserve more attention. The messier the history, the better! Wait... THAT'S Classical? Have you ever recognized classical music in a movie, commercial, TV show, video game, or pop song? I love finding these connections, so please send them my way! Behind the Curtain: Questions about what it's actually like to study music, perform opera, or work in the classical music industry. Or maybe there's something about the industry that you think deserves more attention. Dear Practice Room Tea: Questions, dilemmas, advice, or something you've been dying to get off your chest. I'd love to bring some of these into conversations with guests on the podcast. Please feel free to share anything in the comments! You absolutely don't have to be a musician to participate. Honestly, I'd especially love to hear from people who don't know much about classical music because part of the reason I'm doing this is to introduce more people to this slightly ridiculous world. If you have a story you'd rather not share publicly, you're more than welcome to message me privately! Just let me know if you'd like to stay anonymous. Please avoid including identifying details about other people, and I'll always ask before sharing personal stories on the podcast. I'm really excited (and honestly a little nervous) to finally get this going. I've wanted to do something like this for a while, and I'm hoping this can become a fun little corner of Reddit where we can talk about classical music without taking ourselves too seriously. Thank you for being here, especially if you're joining before I've even released an episode! I can't wait to hear everyone's stories and start spilling the tea in December. — Ayla Rose Practice Room Tea | Spilling the Tea, One Note at a Time.

This December, I'm dedicating the final special edition of Built America Magazine for 2026 to something deeply personal to me. I'm not only a publisher. I'm also the mother of a Make-A-Wish child. I've seen firsthand what happens when complete strangers come together to bring something extraordinary into a child's life. When you're a parent facing circumstances you would give anything to change, those moments mean more than words can explain. My connection to construction is personal, too. A bad contractor experience during my childhood taught me how deeply the people we trust with our homes can affect our lives. It's one of the reasons integrity, accountability, and genuine care have always mattered so much to me in this industry. And that's where these two parts of my life come together. BUILDING WISHES is about the people in our industry who make a difference in someone else's life, often without realizing just how much it means. My vision is to bring together wish-granting organizations supporting critically ill children, educational organizations helping students find their future in construction, and the businesses and individuals throughout our built environment who genuinely care about the people they serve. Wondering if your company belongs in this edition? Have you ever dedicated a project to someone or helped a family who needed it? Do you manufacture a product that saves lives, changes lives, or makes someone's everyday world a little easier? Are you a homebuilder who understands you're not just building a house, but the place where someone's children will grow up? Or maybe you're a family-owned lumberyard or building materials supplier who still knows your customers by name and takes pride in being part of what they're building. That's my dream for Building Wishes. From the smallest family-owned business to the largest manufacturer, developer, or construction company, I want to hear the stories of people who remember that behind every project, product, and purchase, there's a person whose life we're touching. As we begin bringing this December edition together, I'd love to hear from organizations, companies, and individuals who see themselves in this vision. And if you know someone whose story deserves to be told, please reach out. Sometimes, the most meaningful thing we build isn't a structure at all. adults-who-chose-unconventional-paths-li.core: Posted in last 7 days Adults Who Chose Unconventional Paths - Life Reinvention Stories When I Look at the World Have you ever loved a song for decades, only to hear it one day and realize it means something entirely different? That happened to me this morning. I was running errands when U2's When I Look at the World came on. It's from All That You Can't Leave Behind, an album I played relentlessly while driving across the country to New Mexico for a job in my mid-twenties. At the time, I was leaving behind a relationship that hadn't worked out. Everyone around me seemed to be finding their long-term partners, getting married, and following the expected script. Meanwhile, I was packing up and driving somewhere I'd never been. Another milestone missed. Another reminder that my life wasn't following the rules. I spent evenings watching sunsets over the Southwestern desert, often finding a hill where I could park and take it all in. Back then, that song felt like it was about seeing something other people couldn't. But underneath it was a familiar question: What was wrong with me? Because for much of my life, I'd assumed there must be something. Fast-forward a few decades and one late ADHD diagnosis. Today, I heard that song entirely differently. I heard a lifetime of masking. Trying to think, communicate, and experience the world the way everyone else seemed to. The exhaustion of trying to fit into expectations I hadn't even realized I was following. And I felt grief. Not because my brain works differently, but because I spent so many years believing that difference was a deficiency. What might my life have looked like if I'd understood my brain sooner? If I'd recognized that seeing patterns, connecting seemingly unrelated information, anticipating outcomes, and working backward from the big picture weren't weaknesses? The things that made me feel like a misfit were also some of my greatest strengths. And here's what fascinates me. That twenty-something woman driving alone across the country didn't know any of this. She didn't understand ADHD or masking. She just knew that staying somewhere because it was familiar wasn't a good enough reason to stay. Thank goodness she kept going. Because all those unexpected turns eventually led me to a life I didn't even know I wanted. My Misfit Life. A life where other people's expectations are no longer mine to carry. People can come along for the ride or not. I'm still taking the trip. Even if I have to board every airplane or drive every car alone. Now I want to hear YOUR story. Have you ever reached a fork in the road where everyone else turned right, but something inside you told you to go left? Changed careers? Left a relationship? Started over? Discovered something about yourself that changed everything? I'm looking for guests for the My Misfit Life podcast. Interested? Email [email redacted] with the subject "My Misfit Story." Tell me about the road you took and what you discovered. My Misfit Life

undiscovered-industry-talent-how-to-get-.core: Posted in last 7 days Undiscovered Industry Talent - How to Get Featured by Journalists One of the best bits of my job is all the great people I get to speak to (hi, everyone💖). But I'd love to see some new voices in this space, alongside the familiar faces we see every year at conferences and in articles. So, with that in mind, I thought I'd post about how to get featured by an industry journalist…and get asked back again. Hopefully it will inspire some of you to come forward, or to nominate undiscovered talent in your team to take the spotlight: ⭐ The biggest thing is to let us know a) you exist (haha, always helps!) and b) you're interested...tell us you'd like to be in an article or on a podcast, or whatever it is. Otherwise we don't know and can't seek you out. Drop us a LinkedIn DM or an email to introduce yourself. Don’t be shy. We don’t bite! ⭐ Don’t assume you need to be a CFO, group treasurer or conference regular to have something worth saying. You absolutely don’t. We’d love to see more junior people getting some profile too, or people from smaller companies, not just corporate giants. There are no preconceptions from us. ⭐ Pitch us your personal story, things that make you...well, you! Bring your personality and quirks – we love that and it makes storytelling so much more powerful. ⭐️ If you want to talk about an achievement or project, explain why we should care. What did you change? What went wrong? What was difficult? What did you learn? Give us something to get our teeth into, not just all the good bits. 🧡 And finally, just be a nice person!! Journalists are doing a tough job (criticism is a big part of it), with a lot of responsibility and, generally, not a huge amount of money (the average annual salary for newspaper and magazine writers/reporters in the UK is £28,429). We ALWAYS remember the people who are lovely to work with! I've popped some more advice (as well as some things NOT to do when working with industry journalists), in the carousel. Hopefully these are helpful. If not, just enjoy the pictures of Clara the poodle puppy that I squeezed in there as well 😄 Any questions about how to get featured (even by another journalist, not me), how to come across well, your right to review, or anything else, please drop me a line or leave a comment below. families-of-madras-presidency-wwii-servi.author: Adhaar Kaul
families-of-madras-presidency-wwii-servi.core: Posted in last 7 days Families of Madras Presidency WWII Servicemen - Records & Memories 833,701 men. Nobody in the room had heard that number before Saturday. For eighty years the story has been that India’s army came from the Punjab and the hills, and that the South stayed at home. The archives say otherwise. On Saturday I said so. I was the invited guest speaker at the Open Meeting of the Families In British India Society at the Union Jack Club in London. The talk: “The Madras Presidency’s and South Indian States’ Forgotten Contribution to the British Empire”. My talk in London and, as far as I can find, the first anywhere to tell this story whole. Still no book on it. Between 1939 and 1945 the Madras Presidency and the South Indian States put 833,701 men into the war: soldiers, sailors and airmen, the States’ own forces, and the men of the labour units behind the Burma front. More than any other part of India, the Punjab included. Between March 1943 and the end of 1944, 2,825 of the 6,148 sailors the Royal Indian Navy added, 45.9 per cent, came from the Southern Provinces. That is from Vice-Admiral Godfrey’s confidential report at the Imperial War Museum. At the British Library I found the original of a figure I had only seen quoted: from March 1942 Travancore, Cochin and Pudukkottai raised 179 labour units for the Army, “involving more than 150,000 men”, the Resident for the Madras States, January 1945. Their blood, their sweat and their bones are in Iraq and the Middle East, in Italy and in Burma: “from Italy to Sumatra”, as the Commander-in-Chief himself wrote. In London there are statues for the Gurkha and for the Sikh soldier, and they deserve them. For the men of the South there is nothing with their name on it. In February 1945 Sir Stafford Cripps cabled Madras that its gift of fighter squadrons to the RAF “will always be remembered with gratitude”. Britain wrote that down. Then it forgot. I am going to hold it to its word. This will not be one talk and then silence. Every week until VJ Day, 15 August 2027, I will post one piece of evidence until these men have the honour they are owed and a place in Britain’s memory. Then an exhibition. Thank you to FIBIS and Mike Tickner for the invitation and the day, to the National Army Museum, The National Archives, UK, The British Library and Imperial War Museums, and to my mentor, Mr. N. Mishra, DIS, an alumnus of the Royal Military College of Science and the University of Oxford, who has been an elder brother more than a mentor. Can you help? If someone in your family served in a Madras unit, the Royal Indian Navy or the air forces, in the Second World War or before, I want to hear about them: letters, photographs, medals, memories. Email and QR code on the handout. If you think these men should be remembered, repost this; one family who sees it may be keeping the letters. The South’s forgotten service, no. 1 of a weekly series to VJ Day 2027. Next: Wednesday. #MadrasPresidency #ForgottenContribution #IndianArmy #MilitaryHistory #FamilyHistory #Remembrance
